Abstract (英文): Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

</details>

Abstract (英文): Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

Abstract (英文): Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. We look for a mathematical structure weak enough to cover any such case and strong enough to support general theorems, so that results follow from the structure's conditions rather than from a particular pipeline or criterion. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. The framework allows one to address systematically questions of symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization, and we establish what the structure settles in each case before any particular criterion of identity is chosen.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Financial agents produce numerical claims that can be wrong even when their calculations execute correctly, due to mismatched reporting periods, unsupported sources, incompatible units, or incorrect financial definitions. We introduce FinVerify, an evidence-grounded framework for verifying financial agents' numerical claims. Based on an analysis of 190 incorrect trajectories from the Agent Finance Reasoning dataset, we define five error categories--temporal integrity, source fidelity, comparability, accounting integrity, and financial-model fidelity--and operationalize them as verification protocols. An LLM structures claims and supporting evidence, while deterministic validators check financial requirements; when authoritative formulas are available, Z3 checks consistency with grounded inputs. FinVerify accepts only if all applicable checks pass, rejects proven violations, and abstains when evidence is insufficient. We evaluate the framework against a Direct baseline and an LLM judge across five fixed-candidate benchmarks. On Agent Finance Reasoning, accepted-claim precision increases from 56.4% for the LLM judge to 76.7% at 81.2% coverage. On XBRLFiling, FinVerify achieves 99.8% accepted-claim precision and 97.0% decision accuracy; on FinanceBench-67, it reaches 87.9% accepted-claim precision versus 69.7% for the judge. Improvements are smaller on FinQA and TAT-QA, where authoritative evidence is limited. These results suggest that explicit, evidence-backed verification can improve financial-agent reliability while exposing trade-offs between correctness, false rejection, and abstention.

Abstract (英文): We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.

Abstract (英文): GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Abstract (英文): Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.

Abstract (英文): An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs) activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all the experts in GPU memory for high efficiency. Expert pruning reduces this GPU memory footprint cost, yet discards the contribution of pruned experts. Existing remedies either rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training. In this paper, we find that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. Abstract (英文): For Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) users, effective sound awareness goes beyond detecting \emph{what} sound occurs; it requires understanding \emph{what it means}, \emph{how urgent it is}, and \emph{what to do}. However, existing mobile assistants largely reduce acoustic scenes to isolated labels or generic alerts, failing to provide contextual guidance when the same sound implies different risks across scenarios. We present \sysname, a mobile hearing assistant agent that closes the sensing--reasoning--action loop for \textit{scenario-aware} and \textit{personalized} DHH assistance. \sysname adopts a \textit{neuro-symbolic} design that transforms continuous acoustic and physical context streams into structured intermediate representations (IRs) for controllable reasoning and guidance. It introduces three key mechanisms. \textit{First}, a perception-thresholded sensing mechanism enables energy-efficient always-on awareness by activating processing only for perceptually meaningful events while preserving safety-critical cues through deterministic overrides. \textit{Second}, a staged neuro-symbolic reasoning framework performs promptless scenario understanding by conditioning an on-device audio-language model on structured IRs instead of user-authored context descriptions. \textit{Third}, a bounded human-in-the-loop personalization mechanism adapts user-specific guidance through lightweight on-device decision-boundary updates while preserving population-aligned reasoning. We evaluate \sysname on smartphones and in-vehicle systems across diverse scenarios. It achieves favorable accuracy--latency--energy tradeoffs and personalized guidance.

Abstract (英文): Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.

Abstract (英文): Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

Abstract (英文): Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

Abstract (英文): Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

</details>

Abstract (英文): The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists.
  We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

Abstract (英文): Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

Abstract (英文): In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. Abstract (英文): Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

Abstract (英文): Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

</details>

Abstract (英文): LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.

</details>

Abstract (英文): This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

Abstract (英文): We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

Abstract (英文): In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

Abstract (英文): Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

Abstract (英文): We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

Abstract (英文): UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection. However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. Analysis based on the orthophoto alone is therefore structurally insufficient. We address this by detecting objects on the individual images and merging redundant detections across them. This task lies between multi-object tracking and re-identification, as mapping flights form temporally ordered but sparsely sampled sequences with object reappearances across flight strips. We fine-tune YOLO detectors on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection operations, roughly doubling mAP50 over the previous system, and propose re-identification approaches based on 3D positions from sparse reconstruction, DINOv3 appearance embeddings, and their combination via constrained greedy clustering. %On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, the combined weighted multi-pass approach achieves the best trade-off between association accuracy and count error. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, an association-only evaluation using ground-truth detections shows that the combined weighted multi-pass approach provides the best trade-off between association quality and count error. Abstract (英文): Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

Abstract (英文): Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

Abstract (英文): Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. Abstract (英文): Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context.
  Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

Abstract (英文): We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.

One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Abstract (英文): Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

</details>

Abstract (英文): AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged

Abstract (英文): Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

</details>

Abstract (英文): Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

</details>

Abstract (英文): When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

</details>

On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Abstract (英文): We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. Abstract (英文): Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

Abstract (英文): Accurate inundated landscape mapping is essential for understanding hydrological connectivity, wetland dynamics and floodplain processes in tropical environments. However, optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors often produce inconsistent inundation estimates due to differences in sensor physics, wavelength sensitivity, vegetation and cloud penetration, and analytical methods. These challenges are amplified in wet–dry tropical systems, where cloud cover, heterogeneous vegetation and seasonal flooding complicate water detection. This study develops a unified multi-sensor framework for comparing and integrating inundation products derived from Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 C-band and PALSAR-2 L-band SAR in the Daly River floodplain system in northern Australia. Inundated landscape maps were generated using supervised Random Forest classification and unsupervised multi-Otsu thresholding, followed by multi-sensor fusion analysis. Products were developed and validated using wet- and dry-season field observations and Indigenous Knowledges. Results showed strong seasonal and sensor-specific differences. Sentinel-2 provided the most balanced representation of dry-season floodplain vegetation and inundation, while Sentinel-1 achieved high wet-season overall accuracy (>0.95) under cloud-affected conditions. PALSAR-2 improved the detection of inundated vegetation and structurally complex environments, reaching an overall accuracy of 0.97. Multi-sensor evidential reasoning (fusion) improved spatial coherence and class delineation, but performance varied across sensor combinations. These findings show that optical, C-band SAR and L-band SAR inundation products are not directly interchangeable in tropical wetlands. Instead, they performed separately for each landscape. The proposed framework supports the comparison and integration of multi-sensor inundation products to enhance wetland conservation initiatives, wetland monitoring, hydrological assessment, and environmental management in data-limited tropical regions globally.

Abstract (英文): Arctic sea ice fragmentation involves changes in floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity, which affect lateral melt rates and ice–ocean heat fluxes. Existing metrics primarily characterize floe size distributions or area fractions, limiting their capacity to resolve variations in the spatial arrangement of floes. We propose a spatial floe fragmentation index (SFFI) that jointly quantifies floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity. Using 416 Sentinel-1 SAR scenes spanning diverse Arctic regions and ice conditions, we extract floe contours to generate 52,074 SFFI reference labels. For samples with comparable floe area composition, higher SFFI values correspond to greater inter-floe spacing and lower circularity, demonstrating that the index captures spatial and geometric differences not represented by area composition alone. To enable daily Arctic monitoring, we develop a neighborhood-aware retrieval framework integrating AMSR2 radiometry, sea ice concentration (SIC), and neighborhood statistics, and evaluate its performance using random forest, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models. Under the 2016–2024 SAR-scene split, XGBoost with the complete feature set achieves the best performance, with an R2 of 0.6877, an RMSE of 0.3454, and an MAE of 0.2536. Neighborhood-aware features provide relative R2 gains of 4.6% to 10.0% over the SIC-inclusive baselines. The selected model maintained robust predictive performance on the independent 2025 dataset, supporting its temporal transferability. Using the best-performing model, we generate a daily Arctic SFFI product on a 12.5 km grid for 2016–2025. Results show that SFFI captures a pronounced seasonal cycle, with high-SFFI areas expanding during the melt season and contracting during refreezing, while revealing regional differences among Arctic marginal seas.

Abstract (英文): The comparability between satellite-based and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) imagery is critical for multiscale forest monitoring. It enables the integration of fine-resolution observations into a broader satellite-derived spatial and temporal context. Understanding this comparability supports the strategic use of centimeter-resolution UAS data to address fine-scale ecological questions, to serve as gap-filling observations within satellite-based time series during periods of absent data retrievals, and to link fine-scale canopy structural variation to landscape-level vegetation dynamics observed from space. This study investigated the spectral and vegetation index level consistency between Sentinel-2 and UAS multispectral measurements acquired over a 300 ha managed broadleaved forest in Central Europe. UAS data were collected using a fixed-wing platform equipped with a MicaSense Altum multispectral sensor and temporally matched to Sentinel-2 overpasses over a 6-month period at approximately two-week intervals. Cross-platform agreement was quantified using distribution-based similarity metrics, spatial aggregation of UAS data to Sentinel-2 spatial resolution, intrinsic correlation analysis, and single-date regression modeling. At their native spatial resolutions, UAS observations exhibited systematically higher radiometric variability and stronger distributional asymmetry than Sentinel-2 data, particularly in the red-edge band, consistent with increased sensitivity to fine-scale illumination differences and canopy structural heterogeneity, and partly reflecting radiometric differences between individual UAS flights. Spatial aggregation of UAS data reduced this variability but did not fully remove wavelength-dependent discrepancies, with the highest levels of agreement consistently observed in the green, red, and near-infrared bands. Among the vegetation indices, normalized difference metrics, particularly the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), showed the strongest and most temporally stable cross-platform consistency across both multitemporal distributions and individual acquisition dates. In contrast, simple ratio-based indices and indices incorporating red-edge wavelengths exhibited systematic distributional shifts and reduced temporal robustness. These distributional shifts are consistent with persistent sensor-level spectral response differences rather than index-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings indicate that normalized difference indices built from spectrally well-matched bands, which largely remove radiometric differences between UAS flights, provide a robust basis for the joint exploitation of UAS and Sentinel-2 observations, enabling consistent multiscale monitoring of broadleaved forests while retaining the complementary advantages of each observational platform.

Abstract (英文): High-spatial-resolution (HR) bathymetry is crucial for ensuring navigation safety and effective environmental management in shallow waters. However, traditional bathymetry retrieval from medium-resolution satellites yields large uncertainties under complex substrates and strong spatial heterogeneity. HR sensors, such as PlanetScope SuperDove (~3.7 m), can resolve fine-scale features but often have low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited spectral bands, leading to noisy bathymetry retrievals. To address this challenge, we developed BathyUNet++, a UNet++ architecture enhanced with spatial and channel squeeze & excitation (scSE) attention modules, for bathymetry retrieval from SuperDove imagery. While this architecture effectively leverages spatial context and complementary spectral information, it requires dense training patches. Traditional depth measurements provide sparse spatial coverage, and Airborne LiDAR Bathymetry (ALB) remains geographically limited. Therefore, we adopted a multi-source training strategy that integrates high-resolution ALB data with extensive Landsat 8/9 derived bathymetry to improve the spatial coverage and diversity of training data for SuperDove imagery. In addition, we designed a Central-Region Mean Squared Error (CMSE) that focuses on each patch's center valid receptive field to reduce instability and checkerboard artifacts often seen in satellite products generated via patch-based processing. Independent validation shows that BathyUNet++ achieves high-accuracy bathymetry retrievals, with median absolute percentage differences below 15% compared with independent depth measurements from ICESat-2 and ALB. Notably, BathyUNet++ substantially reduces noise compared with bathymetry maps derived from pixel-based algorithms, yielding spatially consistent bathymetry maps. The proposed framework overcomes the limitations of low-SNR data and can be readily adapted to other HR sensors, offering a promising solution for the broader application of HR bathymetry retrieval in optically shallow waters.

Abstract (英文): Winter wheat yield is shaped by crop growth status and surface hydrological conditions.
